Pending Release Native Intent R11
Problem: release requested by TTL job could become owned by fixed pending-release ring while native tracker still carried `PendingTtl/Releasable` and handle map still carried nonzero TTL. Narrative pinning also set pinned bit without cancelling already staged native release intent or stale pending queue entry. That violates one fact -> one owner and can let pinned or reacquired handle remain release-shaped until later sync.
Solution: Add `ClearNativeReleaseIntent(...)` as single route for clearing tracker byte flags, 64-byte `AssetTrackerDTO.Flags`, map TTL, and float TTL mirror. `QueueExpiredAddressableRelease` now calls it after successful ring enqueue. `SyncNativeRefCountsFromRegistry` calls it when record is reacquired or already owned by pending ring. `SetHeapSanitizerPin` now clears pending/releasable state and cancels `AssetRecord.PendingRelease` when pinning. `DrainPendingReleaseQueue` now dependency-gates tracker reads and drops stale reacquired/pinned queue entries without executing `Addressables.Release`.
Rejected Alternatives: Leaving native TTL bits to be cleared on next scheduled job was rejected because pending release ownership must be immediate and singular. Removing stale entries from ring in-place was rejected because queue is simple fixed SPSC-style ring with dequeue-only semantics; bounded stale dequeue is cheaper and avoids second index mutation route. Forcing `JobHandle.Complete()` during queue drain was rejected; drain returns zero if TTL job is still scheduled.
Scalability potential: Low devices avoid release churn and accidental visible-frame unloads when designers pin critical story assets under pressure. Middle/High/Ultra keep longer residency windows without stale release flags shortening cache life.
Hardware Impact: Static estimate only. Adds bounded native-map checks during release drain; no profiler-measured microseconds. Build was not launched after R11 because CPU was 92.5% and 7 `dotnet` processes were active.
Open-Address Map Generation ABA Guard R12
Problem: `RemoveHandleMapEntry` preserved tombstone `Generation`, but `UpsertHandleMapEntry` reset reused slot to generation `1` unless slot was currently occupied with same hash. remove/reinsert cycle could therefore create ABA-looking map entry for generation-checked readers.
Solution: `UpsertHandleMapEntry` now derives `Generation` from current slot state for every insert path, including tombstones and empty slots. It increments prior slot generation and maps wrap-to-zero back to `1`, keeping `0` reserved as never-initialized/default state.
Rejected Alternatives: Leaving generation as cosmetic was rejected because DTO exposes it and stale readers will treat it as validity fact. Adding another managed side table for generations was rejected because it violates fixed Vault-owned open-address map design.
Scalability potential: Low devices avoid stale-slot false positives during aggressive churn and panic eviction; middle/high/ultra keep same fixed map with stronger generation proof and no added allocation.
Hardware Impact: Static estimate only. One integer increment and zero guard on cold/map mutation paths; no per-entry Burst TTL cost and no profiler-measured microseconds claimed. Build was not launched after R12 because CPU sampled at 92.5%.
Orphaned Addressables Slot Release Ownership R13
Problem: `SyncNativeRefCountsFromRegistry` could find active native tracker whose managed `AssetRecord` was already missing, then clear handle pool slot and native map without proving pooled `AsyncOperationHandle` was released. `TryAcquireTrackedHandle` could also return native-cache hit while `_assetRecords` lacked durable owner, making later release calls no-op.
Solution: Missing-record sync now calls `TryReleaseManagedAddressableSlotForOrphan(assetHash, slot)` before clearing tracker/map state. That helper releases or stages slot handle through existing fault/blind release route, then sweeps duplicate hash entries. Native cache-hit now receives address string, reconstructs durable `AssetRecord` from native slot when record table is missing, and rolls tracker flags, TTL, and map entry state back if fixed-table insertion fails.
Rejected Alternatives: Clearing pool slot best-effort was rejected because it destroys last Unity handle route. Adding second orphan list was rejected because it would create another release owner and reintroduce heap pressure. Returning raw cache-hit handle without managed record was rejected because `Release(assetHash)` depends on `_assetRecords`.
Scalability potential: Low devices with scarce blind frames keep deterministic ownership under queue/bridge pressure; middle/high/ultra keep longer residency without orphaning Unity Addressables state.
Hardware Impact: Fault and recovery paths only. Adds bounded scans over fixed handle pool for orphan cleanup and no new hot-path allocation. Microsecond savings are not claimed; this prevents leaked handle accumulation and later unload spikes.
Tombstone Generation Wrap Guard R14
Problem: R12 guarded `UpsertHandleMapEntry` generation wrap, but `RemoveHandleMapEntry` could still increment `uint.MaxValue` to `0`, temporarily producing default never-owned sentinel on tombstone.
Solution: `RemoveHandleMapEntry` now maps wrap-to-zero back to `1`, matching insert-side guard and preserving `0` as uninitialized/default state across remove/reinsert churn.
Rejected Alternatives: Treating wrap as unreachable was rejected because map is designed for long-running survival sessions. Adding wider generation field was rejected because DTO is explicit 64-byte cache-line layout and no extra bytes are available without breaking layout contract.
Scalability potential: No visual tier change. Low devices under aggressive churn and high/ultra long-residency sessions both keep stable generation semantics.
Hardware Impact: One integer increment and one zero branch on map removal only. No Burst TTL cost and no measured profiler claim. Build was not launched after R13/R14 because CPU sampled at 100%.
Hard-Reaper Shutdown Release Fail-Closed R15
Problem: `ReleaseHardReaperAsyncHandles` runs after reset opens explicit blind frame, so normal teardown releases Addressables cache-clean handle. However, method still ignored release helper return and cleared `_hardReaperCleanBundleCacheHandle` unconditionally, leaving brittle call-order dependency.
Solution: Route shutdown cache-clean handle teardown through `TryExecuteOrForceAddressableReleaseFault`. If release or fixed-bridge staging fails, method preserves handle, marks bundle-cache cleanup incomplete, and returns without pretending teardown succeeded.
Rejected Alternatives: Relying on reset call order was rejected because future callers could reuse helper without explicit blind-frame window. Adding second emergency handle store was rejected because existing fault/blind route already provides one release owner.
Scalability potential: Low devices with scarce blind frames and high pressure keep release ownership even during shutdown/reset. Middle/high/ultra behavior is unchanged.
Hardware Impact: Shutdown/fault path only. No steady-frame cost; it adds one fault-route check before clearing hard-reaper handle. Build was not launched after R15 because CPU sampled at 100%.
Hard-Reaper Completion Release Fail-Closed R16
Problem: `PurgeAddressableCachesAsync` and `HandleHardReaperCleanBundleCacheCompleted` preflighted `CanAcceptAddressableRelease(...)` but still ignored actual `TryExecuteOrDeferBlindFrameRelease(...)` return. future bridge mutation, duplicate callback, or occupied owner field could clear or drop completed `CleanBundleCache` handle after failed stage.
Solution: Treat helper return as authoritative. Field-owned cache-clean handles stay in `_hardReaperCleanBundleCacheHandle` and keep `_hardReaperBundleCacheCleanComplete=false` if release/staging fails. Stray completed callback handles are stored in field when it is empty; if another field-owned handle already exists, stray no-owner handle is discharged through `TryExecuteOrForceAddressableReleaseFault(...)` instead of being dropped.
Rejected Alternatives: Relying on `CanAcceptAddressableRelease(...)` as proof was rejected because it is only preflight over mutable fixed bridge slots. Dropping stray callback handle was rejected because it violates one fact -> one owner. Adding another cache-clean handle queue was rejected because it creates second release owner and reintroduces capacity ambiguity.
Scalability potential: Low devices with scarce blind frames preserve cache-clean handle ownership and retry instead of leaking during memory pressure. Middle/high/ultra keep same hard-reaper cadence and fixed bridge behavior.
Hardware Impact: Hard-reaper completion path only. Adds boolean checks and, only for stray occupied-field failure, one fault-route release attempt. No steady-frame cost and no profiler-measured microseconds. Build was not launched after R16 because CPU sampled at 100%.
Hard-Reaper Reset Abort Gate R17
Problem: R15 made `ReleaseHardReaperAsyncHandles` fail-closed internally, but `ResetAddressableHeapRuntimeState` still ignored that failure and could continue into `DisposeNativeHandleStorage`, `_assetRecords.Clear()`, and Vault state cleanup while `_hardReaperCleanBundleCacheHandle` still owned live Addressables operation handle.
Solution: Change `ReleaseHardReaperAsyncHandles` to return `bool`. `ResetAddressableHeapRuntimeState` now aborts before clearing Vault state or managed records if hard-reaper handle release/staging fails. failure writes existing telemetry dump path and keeps handle field intact for later retry instead of pretending reset ownership was discharged.

Forcing second emergency storage route was rejected; existing fault/blind release route is one owner path. Ignoring this as "shutdown only" was rejected because reset is exactly where lost release ownership is most expensive.
Scalability potential: Low devices under scarce blind frames avoid partial reset leaks. Middle/high/ultra keep same release cadence and do not pay steady-frame cost.

Reset Blind-Window Abort Closure R18
Problem: Reset opens `_explicitBlindFrameWindowActive` before releasing hard-reaper and Addressables storage. If hard-reaper teardown or native handle storage disposal aborted, method returned before clearing explicit blind window, turning safe-frame release gate into persistent bypass.
Solution: Both reset abort branches now clear `_explicitBlindFrameWindowActive` and `_explicitBlindFrameWindowUntil` before dumping telemetry and returning. This preserves fail-closed handle owner while preventing subsequent visible frames from being treated as blind release frames.
Rejected Alternatives: Leaving blind window open for "retry" was rejected because it globally weakens Task 08 and can release unrelated handles in visible gameplay. Adding second retry flag was rejected because existing owner fields already preserve release facts.

Reset Release-Window Abort Closure R19
Problem: hard-reaper teardown abort branch returned before normal reset cleanup that clears `_mockScreenFadeToBlackActive` and `_externalVramPanicActive`. failed no-owner fault release could leave external panic window active, again weakening release gate after aborted reset.
Solution: hard-reaper reset abort path now clears explicit blind, mock fade, and external VRAM panic release windows before telemetry dump and return. live hard-reaper handle remains owned by `_hardReaperCleanBundleCacheHandle`; only global release-window state is closed.
Rejected Alternatives: Keeping panic active to help later retry was rejected because it authorizes unrelated visible-frame releases. Retrying immediately in loop was rejected because it risks reset-time stall and violates bounded teardown behavior.
Scalability potential: Low devices avoid visible-frame release after failed reset cleanup. Middle/high/ultra behavior is unchanged.

Fault Release Panic Scope R20
Problem: `TryExecuteOrForceAddressableReleaseFault` used `_externalVramPanicActive=true` with 0.25 second window to force-release no-owner Addressables handle. That solved local leak but globally opened release gate long enough for unrelated pending handles to release in visible frames.
Solution: Save previous external panic state, set panic only for single `TryExecuteOrDeferBlindFrameRelease(handle)` call, then immediately restore previous state. actual `Addressables.Release` route is still same gate helper; panic override is no longer lingering global window.
Rejected Alternatives: Leaving 0.25 second panic window was rejected because one no-owner fault must not authorize unrelated release facts. Adding second direct release call was rejected because Task 08 requires single `Addressables.Release` route.
Scalability potential: Low devices under handle-bridge saturation still get leak-prevention for orphaned handle without flushing unrelated assets. Middle/high/ultra behavior remains bounded and owner-local.
Hardware Impact: Fault path only. Adds two scalar saves and two restores around forced call; no hot-path cost. Build was not launched after R20 because CPU sampled at 100%.
Project-Wide Release Gate Archaeology R21
Problem: project-wide scan after SHINOBU-owned gate hardening still finds direct `Addressables.Release` calls outside `AssetLifecycleGovernor`: bootstrap dependency prewarm/UI teardown, Core content/VFX prewarm and bundle table ownership, `ItemCatalog` world-prefab fallback, and `WorldChunkResidencyManager` chunk/cache-clear fallback paths. Some are cold boot/teardown, but `ContentRuntimeServices.TickVfxPrewarm` and world residency cleanup can execute during runtime.

SHINOBU_101-owned files remain clean: one direct release line inside `TryExecuteOrDeferBlindFrameRelease`, and external chunk/item routes already prefer `GlobalRegistry.AssetLifecycle` when asset hash/governor is available. remaining direct calls need integrator-owned external Addressables release contract because some handles are content-owned and explicitly documented as not owned by `AssetLifecycleGovernor`.
Rejected Alternatives: Mass-editing Bootstrap, Core Content, World, and SaveSystem-owned catalog paths to call private SHINOBU helper was rejected. It would create hidden ownership transfer for handles whose lifetime is not represented in Vault map, and it could leak handles if governor is unavailable. Adding second global static release queue was rejected because it creates another owner outside Vault and outside existing governor lifecycle.

Compile Attempt 7 Boundary R22

External Addressables Release Gate R23
Problem: R21 found direct `Addressables.Release(` calls outside SHINOBU-owned governor in `GameBootstrapper`, `ContentRuntimeServices`, `WorldChunkResidencyManager`, and `ItemCatalog`. Some calls were cold boot/teardown, but content VFX prewarm, bundle VRAM eviction, and world cache-clear polling can run during gameplay cadence. Leaving them direct preserves release-stutter bypass and invalidates project-wide single-route proof.
Solution: Added two narrow owner methods on existing `AssetLifecycleGovernor`: `TryStageExternalAddressableRelease(...)` for handles that still have domain owner and can be retained on failure, and `TryReleaseExternalAddressableFault(...)` for already-ownerless failure handles that would otherwise leak. Core Content, World residency, ItemCatalog fallback, and Bootstrap dependency prewarm now call those methods instead of `Addressables.Release(`. Owned tables clear their handle slot only after governor accepts release/staging. No-owner paths use existing single-call fault route, which still funnels through same gated `TryExecuteOrDeferBlindFrameRelease` body.
Rejected Alternatives: second static release queue was rejected because it creates another global owner outside Vault/gov lifecycle. Keeping direct release in cold Bootstrap was rejected because it leaves static proof ambiguous and encourages copy/paste into runtime paths. Routing `Addressables.ReleaseInstance` through this path was rejected because UI prefab instances require Unity's instance-release API and are not equivalent to raw dependency/asset handles.
Scalability potential: Low devices get fewer visible-frame unload stalls because content/world fallbacks now share blind-frame bridge. Middle/High/Ultra preserve larger residency windows while still using one release route. Bootstrap dependency handles may live until governor drains detached release bridge, trading short cold-start residency tail for predictable frame behavior.
Hardware Impact: Static estimate only. change removes direct runtime release calls from Core Content and World polling paths; expected benefit is avoiding driver-level release hitches on MX350/i3-class hardware. No microsecond measurement is claimed because Unity import/profiler proof is absent and compile remains blocked by missing Construction source.

SHINOBU_102 Rationale
Decision 001 - Injection Point
Problem: Valid 64-byte FutureCommandEnvelope packets currently reach `FutureCommandSandboxValidator.DrainPreSimulation()` and are routed by `ValidateFutureCommandEnvelopeJob.RouteEnvelope()`; legacy `ModCommand` lanes are disabled by `LegacyCommandSurfaceEnabled = false`.
Solution: Attach command kernels inside existing FutureCommandSandboxValidator route after integrity/opcode validation and before DevNull fallback. This keeps PRE_SIMULATION timing and preserves SignalBus/DataVault ownership model.
Rejected Alternatives: `IModCommandKernel` was rejected because it is managed interface, legacy-only, and blocked from runtime when future sandbox is active. Direct subsystem calls were rejected because one fact must have one owner.
Scalability potential: Low uses strict queue shedding before kernels run. Middle keeps haptic/subtitle budgets bounded. High/Ultra retain richer haptic/subtitle traffic while still preserving survival priority.
Hardware Impact: Avoids reactivating legacy NativeQueue and interface dispatch. Estimated gain on i3/MX350: 15-40 us on mod-heavy frames versus managed interface dispatch and duplicate queue drain.
Decision 002 - HapticPulse Layout Constraint
Problem: prompt requests `HapticPulseSignal` to be 32 bytes while containing `uint WaveformHash`, `float Intensity`, `float Duration`, and `double3 TargetAUP`. That payload is 36 bytes before padding and 40/48 bytes after ARM64-safe alignment depending on field order.
Solution: Implement smallest ARM64-safe explicit layout that preserves all requested fields without unaligned double loads: `double3 TargetAUP` at offset 0, `uint WaveformHash` at 24, `float Intensity` at 28, `float Duration` at 32, explicit padding to 48-byte multiple of 16. Report impossible 32-byte constraint in audit instead of faking overlapping fields.
Rejected Alternatives: `Pack=1` and field overlap were rejected because they would create unaligned ARM64 access and corrupt semantic payload. Dropping `double3` was rejected because AUP is required by kernel task.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle can suppress haptic signals before they enter downstream lanes. High/Ultra can preserve full AUP context for richer haptic spatialization without changing command format.
Hardware Impact: Prevents two-cache-line unaligned double fetch traps on ARM64. Estimated low-end protection: avoids worst-case 10x load penalty for haptic spam records.
Decision 003 - Dear Lie Haptic Fallback
Problem: Haptic hardware calls are not deterministic gameplay state and can spam expensive platform APIs during thermal pressure or rollback.
Solution: Kernel writes unmanaged camera shake scalar impulse into Vault buffer when `GlobalQualityWeight` collapses or force-fallback tuning flag is set, suppressing haptic SignalBus emission.
Rejected Alternatives: Direct Unity XR/Input haptics were rejected because kernels are Burst/stateless and must not own hardware APIs. Physics-style vibration simulation was rejected as wasted ALU for feedback.
Scalability potential: Low collapses to scalar camera impulse. Middle blends suppression by quality and range. High/Ultra keep haptic signal emission for downstream overkill devices.
Hardware Impact: Estimated i3/MX350/Quest protection: 20-80 us saved during haptic spam bursts by avoiding downstream haptic event fanout.
Decision 004 - Continuous Load Shedding
Problem: existing backlog shedder only dropped from queue head under low-quality gate, which could discard survival commands before decorative haptics/subtitles.
Solution: Add `LoadSheddingJob` with deterministic priority buckets. dynamic budget uses `GlobalQualityWeight^2`; optional haptic/subtitle packets are dropped first, normal packets second, survival overrides last. CSV profile priority weights can override default buckets.
Rejected Alternatives: Random drops and head-only drops were rejected because they are nondeterministic from design perspective and can destroy authoritative survival state while preserving cosmetic spam.
Scalability potential: Low collapses UGC bandwidth aggressively. Middle keeps survival and selected feedback. High/Ultra allow richer haptic/subtitle traffic while still bounded by telemetry-visible budgets.
Hardware Impact: Estimated i3/MX350 gain: 50-300 us on hostile queue bursts by capping validation/routing work to polynomial budget before expensive route loop.
Decision 004A - Observer AUP Source
Problem: Haptic distance checks require local `float3` math, but command envelope stores global `double3 TargetAUP`.
Solution: Resolve observer AUP from `HectonFloatingOrigin.CurrentTotalOffsetDouble` on managed scheduling side, pass it as scalar `double3` into Burst, subtract it from `TargetAUP`, then cast only local delta to `float3`.
Rejected Alternatives: Casting global `TargetAUP` directly to `float3` was rejected because 100km coordinates amplify jitter. Polling player transform from inside job was rejected because Burst jobs must stay pure/unmanaged.
Scalability potential: Low through Ultra all use same deterministic local delta; high-tier richness can happen downstream without changing kernel precision.
Hardware Impact: Prevents precision recovery work and NaN propagation. Estimated saved cost is failure prevention, not steady hot-loop ALU.
Decision 005 - Rollback Freeze Scope
Problem: prior validator rejected all commands while rollback bit 70752:1<<4 was active. That suppresses spam, but it also blocks deterministic survival overrides.
Solution: Move rollback handling into kernel route scope. Haptic and subtitle emissions are suppressed during rollback; survival override still emits its deterministic request signal.
Rejected Alternatives: Keeping global rollback rejection was rejected because it violates task's state determinism requirement. Direct replay of haptic/subtitle after rollback was rejected because UI/audio spam is non-authoritative.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra all preserve deterministic survival state while UI/audio noise remains suppressed during resimulation.
Hardware Impact: Prevents wasted SignalBus/UI/audio fanout during rollback. Estimated low-end gain: 10-60 us on rollback frames with active UGC spam.
Decision 006 - Kernel Telemetry Ring
Problem: Command kernels need postmortem proof for spikes and rejected payloads; generic sandbox telemetry cannot show per-opcode kernel work.
Solution: Allocate vault-owned 300-entry `KernelExecutionTelemetryEntry` ring and dump it to `Docs/AgentLogs/Dump_COMMAND_FORGE.bin` when measured validator/kernel execution exceeds 0.5 ms.
Rejected Alternatives: Managed log strings and chat reports were rejected because they allocate and are not deterministic forensic artifact.
Scalability potential: Low devices expose thermal shedding and haptic fallback counts. High/Ultra expose whether overkill UGC traffic is still under budget.
Hardware Impact: Ring write is one 64-byte store per processed frame; spike dump is cold/fault path only. Expected hot cost below 1 us.
Decision 007 - CSV Human Control
Problem: Kernel priority and max processing budgets must be tunable without recompiling C# or adding managed CSV parsing to gameplay paths.
Solution: Add `kernel_tuning_profiles.csv` and parse it through vault-owned byte scratch into `ModKernelTuningProfile` DTOs using `ReadOnlySpan ` token slicing, ASCII numeric parsing, and FNV-1a opcode hashing.
Rejected Alternatives: `string.Split`, `List `, and reflection-based CSV readers were rejected because play-mode tuning would allocate and hide parser failure modes.
Scalability potential: Low can reduce max haptic/subtitle budgets and priority weights. Middle can keep restrained feedback. High/Ultra can raise optional budgets without changing kernel code.
Hardware Impact: Cold/editor path only. Hot path uses already-hydrated unmanaged DTOs. Expected frame cost: 0 us.
Decision 008 - Editor Facade Scope
Problem: Developers need to verify kernel behavior without compiled mod DLL and without relying on chat logs.
Solution: Add UI Toolkit `Mod Kernel Inspector` that reads 300-frame vault telemetry ring, flashes red on shedding changes, reloads kernel CSV, and injects synthetic 64-byte FutureCommandEnvelope packets through same validator `Request()` route.
Rejected Alternatives: Extending old IMGUI sandbox tuner only was rejected because task explicitly requires UI Toolkit and live command injection for kernel path.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra are observable by changing quality/thermal tuning and watching actual processed/shed/rejected counters instead of assuming behavior.
Hardware Impact: Editor-only. No player hot-path cost.
Decision 009 - Mod API Source Signal Drift
Problem: `Docs/Modding/Validate_Mod_API_Static.ps1` failed after shared worktree gained one additional first-party `ISignal` in `Assets/_Project/Scripts/Core/GlobalSignals.cs`: `HabitatFloodAcousticMuffleSignal`. schema still recorded `160 / 2 / 158`, so mod API static gate rejected source/doc mismatch.
Solution: Update only Modding API schema/audit documentation to schema revision 15 with `161` source signals, `2` projected signals, and `159` denied-by-default signals. Add `HabitatFloodAcousticMuffleSignal` to denied inventory. Do not expose new `SignalBus ` lane to mods.
Rejected Alternatives: Exposing `SignalBus ` was rejected because habitat flood audio muffle data is first-party presentation/DSP coordination and can be spammed or misread as authority. Editing `GlobalSignals.cs` was rejected because this agent does not own source signal and correct mod API response is deny-by-default accounting.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra all keep mod subscription surface unchanged. First-party audio/fluid systems can scale their own DSP; mods remain on sanitized envelopes and projected read-only lanes only.
Hardware Impact: No runtime cost. Static gate protection prevents accidental public callback exposure that could add unbounded managed fanout on low-end hardware.
Decision 010 - Kernel Telemetry Accuracy And Public Legacy Facade Quarantine
Problem: `KernelExecutionTelemetryEntry.HapticFallbacks` was derived from `KernelSuppressed - rollbackSuppressed`, which also counted out-of-range haptic pulses as Dear Lie camera fallback. public `HectonAPI.Commands` legacy methods returned `false`, but lacked same explicit obsolete quarantine marker already present on dispatcher-side legacy methods.
Solution: Add dedicated `FutureCommandValidationStats.HapticFallbacks` field at offset 56 and increment it only inside `WriteCameraJuiceImpulse()`. `RecordKernelTelemetry()` now writes that exact counter instead of inferring from generic suppression. Expand `ValidateLayoutOrDump()` to check `ModKernelTuningProfile` and `ModKernelCameraJuiceState`. Mark `HectonAPI.Commands.Request`, `RequestAup`, and `RequestRenderInstance` obsolete while preserving their `false` return behavior.
Rejected Alternatives: Inferring fallback counts from suppression buckets was rejected because range culling, rollback suppression, and camera fallback are different facts with different owners. Removing public legacy methods was rejected because it would be public API break outside this batch boundary.
Scalability potential: Low devices now report exact scalar-fallback use instead of conflating it with range rejection. Middle/High/Ultra telemetry can distinguish optional haptics that were too far away from feedback intentionally converted into camera juice.
Hardware Impact: One extra 4-byte stats counter inside existing 64-byte cache-line DTO. No hot allocation. Telemetry interpretation avoids wasting optimization time on false haptic fallback counts.
Decision 011 - Standalone Kernel Parity Guard
Problem: primary inlined command router already rejects haptic `TargetAUP` outside `+/-100000m` and accepts both `SubtitleCue` and `TriggerSubtitleCue` opcode aliases. standalone Burst kernel structs are still valuable for direct profiling and injection tests, but they must not silently drift from authoritative route.
Solution: Add same kernel AUP magnitude gate to `HapticPulseKernelJob` before local `float3` conversion. Add `TriggerSubtitleCue` acceptance to `SubtitleCueKernelJob`, preserving numeric-token-only output and rollback suppression.
Rejected Alternatives: Leaving parity to comments was rejected because editor injection path can exercise standalone jobs in isolation. Routing standalone tests through managed wrappers was rejected because it would hide Burst payload behavior and add allocations.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra all get identical validity semantics between inlined hot route and direct kernel smoke tests. Optional subtitle aliases no longer disappear in test-only profiling.
Hardware Impact: One double3 absolute-value and three comparisons in standalone haptic job, already cold/direct-test relative to inlined router. Prevents invalid AUP fanout and avoids downstream corruption recovery cost.
Decision 012 - Active Architecture Mod API Counter Alignment
Problem: active documentation actuality ledger still reported Mod API static gate as `SchemaRevision=14` and `SourceSignals=160` after live validator and Modding docs had moved to `SchemaRevision=15` and `SourceSignals=161`.
Solution: Update only stale Mod API gate tuple in `Docs/ARCHITECTURE/HECTON8_DOCUMENTATION_ACTUALITY_LEDGER.md` to match fresh `Validate_Mod_API_Static.ps1` output.
Rejected Alternatives: Leaving stale active authority row was rejected because it would contradict current static gate and confuse future agents. Broad documentation rewrites were rejected because this domain only owns Mod API counter correction.
Scalability potential: No runtime tier impact; this preserves documentation authority so low/high-tier command-kernel decisions are based on current schema counters.
Hardware Impact: Documentation-only. Prevents unnecessary reruns and false schema-drift debugging.
Decision 013 - ThermalSourceSignal Deny-By-Default Schema Drift
Problem: Mod API static validator re-failed with `Source=162 Schema=161`. missing source inventory entry was `ThermalSourceSignal` in `Assets/_Project/Scripts/Core/GlobalSignals.cs`; it was not command-kernel payload and was not projected to mods.
Solution: Update Modding schema and audit documentation to schema revision 16 with source split `162 / 2 / 160`. Add `ThermalSourceSignal` to denied-by-default inventory and high-risk presentation/environment bucket. Align active architecture/binary ledgers to same static validator tuple.
Rejected Alternatives: Adding mod projection lane was rejected because thermal source/environment hazard data is first-party authority and can be abused for hazard spoofing or callback storms. Editing `GlobalSignals.cs` was rejected because SHINOBU_102 does not own that source signal.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra keep same mod projection surface. First-party thermal systems can scale independently; mods continue through sanitized envelopes and projected read-only lanes only.
Hardware Impact: No runtime cost. Prevents static gate churn and accidental public callback exposure for high-volume environmental signal.
Decision 014 - Compile-Wall Boundary Audit
Problem: ModdingAPI folder currently has no local `.asmdef`, and legacy public facade files in same folder still contain historical direct `using` references to World, Gameplay, Physics, Caves, SaveSystem, UI, Input, and Localization domains. Creating new assembly boundary in this pass would be broad public API migration and could break other agents' work.
Solution: Constrain SHINOBU_102 kernel route to `FutureCommandSandboxValidator.cs`, `ModSpatialContracts.cs`, and editor inspector. new validator's HECTON references are limited to `Hecton8.Core`, `Hecton8.Core.Contracts.Signals`, and `Hecton8.Core.Memory`; focused grep found no World/Gameplay/Physics/Caves/Localization references in new kernel validator/editor/contracts path. Legacy sibling-domain facades remain obsolete and hard-blocked from active command execution.
Rejected Alternatives: Adding new ModdingAPI runtime asmdef was rejected because this folder is existing public API surface with many historical sibling references and no local assembly split; that belongs to Integrator/assembly-routing owner, not to this command-kernel patch. Refactoring legacy facade usings was rejected because legacy surface is already disabled and broad edits would increase compile-wall blast radius.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra runtime kernel behavior is unchanged. This protects iteration scalability by keeping new Burst command path isolated from sibling-domain compile churn.
Hardware Impact: Runtime impact is 0 us. Developer-hardware impact is containment: no new sibling-domain dependency was introduced by command-kernel route, avoiding unnecessary recompilation fanout.
Decision 015 - Exact AUP Violation Telemetry
Problem: `KernelExecutionTelemetryEntry.AupViolations` was populated as boolean derived from rejection mask. Under malicious AUP spam burst, blackbox ring would show only "some AUP violation happened" instead of exact count for that frame.
Solution: Consume final 4-byte slot in `FutureCommandValidationStats` at offset 60 as `AupViolations`. Increment it for global sandbox AUP gate and for three haptic-local AUP gates before writing exact value into `KernelExecutionTelemetryEntry.AupViolations`.
Rejected Alternatives: Keeping bit flag was rejected because 300-frame forensic telemetry must support spike triage, not just category presence. Adding new DTO was rejected because existing 64-byte cache-line stats DTO already had one reserved uint slot.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra runtime behavior is unchanged. QA and endurance bots can now separate single corrupt packet from sustained malicious coordinate spam.
Hardware Impact: One additional uint increment per AUP rejection only. Hot valid-packet cost is 0 us; fault-path forensic resolution improves without changing cache-line size.
Decision 016 - Designer Kernel Profile Consumption
Problem: `kernel_tuning_profiles.csv` hydrated `RangeMeters`, `MaxDurationSeconds`, `IntensityScale`, and per-opcode flags, but hot haptic/subtitle routes only used profile data for priority/budget shedding. That left designer-facing tuning partially inert.
Solution: Pass vault-owned `ModKernelTuningProfile` array into validator Burst job and standalone haptic/subtitle profiling jobs. Haptic pulses now use profile range as hard cap/default, profile max duration as duration cap, profile intensity scale before inverse-square attenuation, and profile flags for camera-juice fallback. Subtitle cues now use profile max duration; `TriggerSubtitleCue` resolves `SubtitleCue` profile alias.
Rejected Alternatives: Managed dictionary lookup was rejected because it would allocate/virtual-dispatch outside Burst. Baking per-opcode constants into C# was rejected because designers need CSV control without recompilation.
Scalability potential: Low can cap haptic range/duration/intensity through CSV while preserving survival priority. Middle can keep restrained presentation traffic. High/Ultra can raise cosmetic range and duration without touching code.
Hardware Impact: Adds bounded linear scan over small vault profile array inside optional haptic/subtitle routes only. Expected cost is below 1 us for current 3-row profile and buys real designer-controlled load shedding.
Decision 017 - Per-Opcode MaxPerFrame Enforcement
Problem: `ModKernelTuningProfile.MaxPerFrame` reduced aggregate command budget, but it did not cap each opcode independently. queue made only of one cosmetic opcode could stay below global budget and still exceed designer's per-opcode spam ceiling.
Solution: Run `LoadSheddingJob` when pending count exceeds smallest active profile cap, even if global budget is not exceeded. Inside Burst, normalize `TriggerSubtitleCue` to `SubtitleCue`, track kept counts for `SurvivalOverride`, `HapticPulse`, and `SubtitleCue`, and drop packets after each opcode reaches its `MaxPerFrame`. Overflow shedding still runs first: optional haptic/subtitle are dropped before standard packets, survival last.
Rejected Alternatives: Managed dictionaries and LINQ grouping were rejected because shedder is pre-simulation hot path. second queue per opcode was rejected because it adds persistent state and Vault fragmentation risk. Head-only dropping was rejected because it can preserve cosmetic spam while discarding survival requests.
Scalability potential: Low devices now enforce both continuous quality-scaled global budget and designer opcode caps. Middle tiers keep bounded haptic/subtitle throughput. High/Ultra can raise CSV caps without changing code, while survival retains highest priority under overflow.
Hardware Impact: Adds one bounded queue scan only when pending count can exceed either global budget or smallest profile cap. Expected low-end protection is 20-120 us on single-opcode spam bursts by preventing optional command fanout from reaching validation and signal lanes.
Decision 018 - Exact Profile Cap Early-Out
Problem: first per-opcode cap patch triggered `LoadSheddingJob` when pending count exceeded smallest active profile cap, but job's early-out compared total queue length to every opcode cap. That was correct for safety, yet it could compact-copy mixed queue even when no individual opcode exceeded its cap.
Solution: During first Burst scan, count priority buckets and exact normalized opcode counts for `SurvivalOverride`, `HapticPulse`, and `SubtitleCue`. Return before compact-copy when there is no aggregate overflow and no exact opcode count exceeds its cap. Keep second pass only for actual overflow or real per-opcode shedding.
Rejected Alternatives: Scanning ring on managed scheduling side was rejected because it duplicates hot-path logic outside Burst and increases main-thread work. Keeping coarse early-out was rejected because it wastes memory bandwidth on mixed queues. Splitting queues by opcode was rejected because it adds persistent state and complicates rollback ordering.
Scalability potential: Low devices still get strict spam shedding. Middle/High/Ultra avoid unnecessary queue copies when small cap exists for different opcode, preserving optional bandwidth without extra memory traffic.
Hardware Impact: Saves one compact-copy pass on mixed queues above smallest profile cap but below their exact opcode caps. Expected protection is 5-40 us on MX350/i3 spam-heavy editor tests, with correctness unchanged.
Decision 019 - Pending Ring Overflow Telemetry
Problem: `EnqueuePendingEnvelope()` protected bounded pending ring by dropping oldest packet when full, but that drop happened before pre-simulation validation and was not counted in kernel telemetry. queue was memory-safe, yet blackbox underreported hostile enqueue spam.
Solution: Reuse 4-byte reserved slot at `ModSandboxRingState` offset 44 as `PendingOverflowDropped`. Increment it with saturation whenever enqueue advances `PendingHead` to make room. At pre-simulation preparation, move counter into existing dropped telemetry path, reset ring counter, and saturating-add it to `LoadSheddingJob` drops.
Rejected Alternatives: Expanding ring-state DTO was rejected because it would break 64-byte cache-line layout. Emitting rejection signal from enqueue was rejected because enqueue can be called from external queue ingestion and must stay bounded/simple. Allocating separate overflow telemetry array was rejected because ring state had unused aligned slot.
Scalability potential: Low devices get accurate proof when spam exceeds ring capacity before quality shedder can run. Middle/High/Ultra can still tolerate larger queues, but hostile overflow is now visible in same 300-frame blackbox.
Hardware Impact: One saturating uint increment only on full-ring enqueue. Valid non-overflow enqueue cost is unchanged. Forensic value is high: queue overflow no longer disappears from telemetry.
Decision 020 - Dead Head-Drop Shedder Removal
Problem: private `DropThermalBacklog()` method remained in validator after priority-based `LoadSheddingJob` became active route. It was unused, but its algorithm was head-only thermal dropping and could reintroduce survival-before-haptic loss if revived later.
Solution: Remove dead private method. only active backlog shedding route is now `LoadSheddingJob`, which applies aggregate quality budget, profile priority buckets, exact per-opcode caps, and survival-last dropping.
Rejected Alternatives: Marking method obsolete was rejected because private dead code still creates misleading local implementation option. Keeping it for fallback was rejected because emergency fallback is opcode map, not inferior shedder.
Scalability potential: Low devices keep deterministic optional-first shedding. Middle/High/Ultra avoid divergent command-drop semantics between two code paths.
Hardware Impact: Runtime cost change is 0 us because method was unused. gain is architectural: one incorrect future branch removed from command-kernel surface.
Decision 021 - Editor Inspector Cadence Throttle
Problem: `ModKernelInspectorWindow` scanned 300-entry kernel telemetry ring and rewrote UI labels on every `EditorApplication.update`. This is editor-only, but it still adds unnecessary iteration-loop noise on developer hardware.
Solution: Add 0.10 second refresh interval using `EditorApplication.timeSinceStartup`. inspector still feels live, but telemetry scans, label string writes, and histogram repaints are capped at 10 Hz.
Rejected Alternatives: Removing live updates was rejected because Task 18 requires real-time histogram feedback. Moving editor window to runtime UI/TMP was rejected because this is editor facade, not in-game UI. Complex zero-string UI formatting was rejected because UI Toolkit labels consume managed strings and path is editor-only.
Scalability potential: Low developer machines get lower editor overhead while observing spam tests. High/Ultra workstations still see enough temporal resolution to tune shedder thresholds.
Hardware Impact: Reduces editor telemetry scan and repaint cadence from typical 60Hz+ to 10Hz. Estimated editor-loop savings: 5-80 us per open inspector frame depending on Unity editor load and repaint cost; player runtime impact is 0 us.
Decision 022 - Editor Inspector Idempotent Subscription
Problem: UI Toolkit can recreate `EditorWindow` visual tree without same lifecycle shape as play-mode components. `CreateGUI()` subscribed to `EditorApplication.update` with `+= Tick` and relied on `OnDisable()` for cleanup, leaving duplicate-subscription risk after UI rebuilds.
Solution: Make subscription idempotent by calling `EditorApplication.update -= Tick` immediately before `+= Tick`, then reset `_nextRefreshTime` so recreated inspector paints once without waiting for previous cadence boundary.
Rejected Alternatives: static global subscription flag was rejected because multiple inspector windows would fight over one flag. Removing update subscription was rejected because Task 18 requires live telemetry. Polling inside IMGUI was rejected because facade is UI Toolkit by assignment.
Scalability potential: Low developer machines avoid duplicated editor polling after UI rebuilds. High/Ultra machines retain live telemetry without accumulating hidden update delegates.
Hardware Impact: Prevents accidental N-times editor telemetry scans/repaints after window rebuild. Runtime player impact is 0 us.
Decision 023 - Self-Audit Overflow And Exact AUP Probe
Problem: `RunSelfAudit()` verified malformed AUP and malformed payload rejection, but it did not verify new exact AUP counter or pending-ring overflow telemetry. That left self-audit weaker than runtime blackbox contract.
Solution: Extend `RunSelfAudit()` with two cold checks: require `stats.AupViolations == 1` for NaN AUP probe, and run local `ModSandboxRingState` overflow probe against staging buffer to confirm `PendingOverflowDropped` saturates and head advancement preserves bounded capacity. probe does not touch real pending ring state.
Rejected Alternatives: Enqueuing thousands of real packets into pending ring was rejected because self-audit must not perturb runtime queues. Adding separate test-only NativeArray was rejected because staging already provides Vault-backed buffer. Ignoring counter was rejected because blackbox telemetry must be testable.
Scalability potential: Low-through-Ultra behavior is unchanged at runtime. editor self-audit now catches telemetry regressions before spam tests hide queue pressure.
Hardware Impact: Cold self-audit only. Runtime hot path impact is 0 us.
Decision 024 - No-Work Kernel Telemetry
Problem: `TryPrepareValidationJob()` recorded generic sandbox telemetry when no commands drained, but it returned before writing command-kernel 300-frame ring. Pure spam frames that only caused enqueue overflow or pre-drain shedding could be absent from `KernelExecutionTelemetryEntry`.
Solution: In no-drain path, synthesize zero-work `FutureCommandValidationStats` value and call `RecordKernelTelemetry()` with `thermalDropped` and pending depth. If drops occurred, telemetry flags `ThermalShed`; otherwise it records zero-work heartbeat.
Rejected Alternatives: Skipping no-work kernel telemetry was rejected because blackbox forensics must show command pressure even when no envelope survives to validation. Forcing validation job with count zero was rejected because it adds scheduling work for no payload.
Scalability potential: Low devices under hostile spam now expose pre-drain drops in kernel ring. High/Ultra behavior is unchanged except for clearer idle/spam telemetry.
Hardware Impact: One 64-byte kernel telemetry write on no-drain frames when telemetry recording is requested. Expected cost below 1 us; forensic value outweighs cold/no-work write.
Decision 025 - Transactional Kernel Tuning CSV Ingest
Problem: `TryIngestKernelTuningProfilesCsv()` cleared live `ModKernelTuningProfile` vault buffer before proving CSV was valid and within capacity. malformed or oversized tuning file could wipe previous designer budgets or partially apply profile set, causing haptic/subtitle spam ceilings to drift silently.
Solution: Add first-pass validator over existing `ReadOnlySpan ` scratch data. It skips empty/comment/header lines, parses every real row, counts accepted profiles, and rejects file if any row is malformed or if accepted count exceeds vault capacity. Only after that proof does cold path call `MemClearArray(profiles)` and perform second parse/write pass.
Rejected Alternatives: Allocating backup profile array was rejected because vault already owns persistent memory and CSV scratch span is enough for deterministic two-pass validation. Accepting partial CSV success was rejected because one bad tuning row can change command spam behavior. Using `string.Split` or managed CSV libraries was rejected because tuning path must remain allocation-free.
Scalability potential: Low devices keep their last known conservative haptic/subtitle caps if designer edits bad CSV. Middle/High/Ultra keep richer profile budgets only when entire profile file is coherent, preventing partial overkill settings from leaking through.
Hardware Impact: Cold/editor path only. Hot frame cost remains 0 us. two-pass scratch scan adds bounded CSV reload work and prevents low-end frames from losing protective command budgets after bad tuning edit.
Decision 026 - Static Gate Explicit ModAupResponse Layout Acceptance
Problem: Mod API static validator required `ModAupResponse` to be declared as `LayoutKind.Sequential`, but source contract now uses `LayoutKind.Explicit, Size = 64`. source is ARM64-safe and size-pinned; validation regex was stale and failed before comparing 64-byte schema value.
Solution: Change validator regex to accept `LayoutKind.Sequential` or `LayoutKind.Explicit` while still requiring explicit `Size = N` declaration and comparing that size to schema. gate now validates fact that matters: public payload remains fixed 64-byte DTO.
Rejected Alternatives: Reverting `ModAupResponse` back to sequential layout was rejected because explicit field offsets are stronger proof for ARM64/cache-line contracts. Disabling size check was rejected because payload layout drift must remain hard failure.
Scalability potential: No runtime tier behavior changes. static gate now supports safer layout style without false failures.
Hardware Impact: Runtime impact is 0 us. Developer-hardware impact is reduced static-gate churn; ARM64 alignment proof remains enforced by source layout and 64-byte schema comparison.
Decision 027 - Transactional Allowed Opcode CSV Ingest
Problem: `TryIngestAllowedOpcodesCsv()` cleared live opcode allowlist before proving full CSV was valid. If designer or pipeline supplied malformed, duplicate, header-only, or oversized file, method could erase current allowlist and either partially apply rows or replace active list with emergency mock opcodes.
Solution: Add first-pass validator for allowed-opcode CSV. It skips empty/comment/header rows, parses every real row, rejects duplicate opcode hashes, and verifies capacity before live `FutureCommandOpcodeRecord` buffer is cleared. emergency mock remains only bootstrap fallback from `Initialize()`, not silent substitute for bad authoritative file.
Rejected Alternatives: Keeping previous "accepted == 0 => emergency mock" behavior was rejected because malformed authoritative source must fail closed and preserve previous live policy. Allocating backup opcode array was rejected because existing vault buffer and scratch bytes are sufficient for two-pass validation. Allowing duplicate opcode rows was rejected because final flag semantics would become order-dependent.
Scalability potential: Low devices retain last known safe allowlist under bad authoring input, so optional spam cannot be accidentally enabled by partial CSV. Middle/High/Ultra keep richer opcode policies only when entire source validates coherently.
Hardware Impact: Cold/editor reload path only. Hot frame cost is 0 us. first pass is bounded by CSV byte length and protects pre-simulation router from bad allowlist mutation.
Decision 028 - CSV Source Authority And Vault Profile Guard
Problem: `TryReloadAllowedOpcodesCsvFromDisk()` pointed at `Docs/Modding/allowed_opcodes.csv`, but file was absent, so editor reload could never hydrate human-readable allowlist. Both allowed-opcode and tuning-profile reloads also accepted files larger than vault scratch buffer by reading only prefix, which could silently apply truncated authoritative source. scheduler/self-audit passed `KernelProfiles` into Burst jobs without failing if that vault handle failed to resolve.
Solution: Add `Docs/Modding/allowed_opcodes.csv` with exact hex hashes for all 12 `FutureCommandOpcodes` constants. Reject allowed/tuning CSV reloads when `FileStream.Length` is zero or exceeds 16KB scratch buffer, before any scratch read or live-buffer mutation. Require `kernelProfiles.IsCreated` in `TryPrepareValidationJob()` and `RunSelfAudit()`. Extend `Validate_Mod_API_Static.ps1` to parse `FutureCommandOpcodes` and prove CSV has exact, duplicate-free hash set.
Rejected Alternatives: Leaving emergency bootstrap as only allowlist source was rejected because designer/editor control would be fake. Truncating oversized files was rejected because valid prefix can mask missing tail and mutate policy incorrectly. Falling back to empty/default profiles when profile vault is missing was rejected because profile data now participates in active load shedding and haptic/subtitle range/duration math.
Scalability potential: Low devices keep protective opcode and profile budgets unless entire authoring source is coherent. Middle/High/Ultra can expand same CSV policy without C# edits, while static validation prevents source/CSV drift.
Hardware Impact: Cold/editor path only; hot frame cost is 0 us. fail-closed length check avoids bad reload that could remove command shedding caps and cost 50-300 us on hostile mod bursts.
Decision 029 - CSV Change-Control Visibility
Problem: After adding `allowed_opcodes.csv`, Modding contract index and change-control checklist still did not name either command-kernel CSV. That creates hidden authority file: present on disk, but absent from documented edit workflow.
Solution: Add `allowed_opcodes.csv` and `kernel_tuning_profiles.csv` to `Docs/Modding/README.md`, add change-control row for future command envelope allowlist/kernel tuning edits, list both CSVs under audit files, and make `Validate_Mod_API_Static.ps1` require files and documentation links.
Rejected Alternatives: Relying on file discovery was rejected because agents will miss side files under context pressure. Updating only README was rejected because checklist is enforced edit workflow. Adding schema counters for these CSVs was deferred because static validator already proves exact allowlist hash equality and tuning file is editor-authoring policy, not public API projection surface.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra behavior is unchanged. benefit is authoring predictability: device-tier command budgets and opcode allowlists now have visible, guarded maintenance route.
Hardware Impact: Runtime impact is 0 us. Developer-hardware impact is reduced false investigation time because static gate now fails immediately if CSV authority files or links disappear.
Decision 030 - Exact CSV Scratch Read
Problem: `FileStream.Read(Span )` is not contractual full-buffer read. Even after rejecting oversized CSV files, short read could still pass valid prefix to transactional parser and mutate live opcode/profile buffers as if entire file had loaded.
Solution: After each editor CSV read, require `read == readLength` before calling `TryIngestAllowedOpcodesCsv()` or `TryIngestKernelTuningProfilesCsv()`. Any short read fails closed before live vault state changes.
Rejected Alternatives: Looping until EOF was rejected for this editor facade because file size is already known, bounded by scratch capacity, and short read under shared file access is coherence failure that should be retried later, not partially accepted. Accepting prefix data was rejected because it can drop tail rows and weaken command shedding.
Scalability potential: Low devices keep previous protective command policies when CSV file is mid-write or partially readable. Middle/High/Ultra can reload richer policies only after file read is coherent.
Hardware Impact: Cold/editor path only; hot frame cost is 0 us. Prevents partial reload from removing per-opcode caps and exposing 50-300 us spam-frame regressions.
Decision 031 - PRE_SIMULATION Profile Lookup Collapse
Problem: `TryPrepareValidationJob()` already resolved `ModKernelTuningProfile` vault buffer, but `ResolveKernelProfileFrameBudget()` and `ResolveSmallestKernelProfileFrameBudget()` resolved same handle again. That is not GC problem, but it is redundant main-thread service/vault lookup inside PRE_SIMULATION scheduling.
Solution: Change both budget helpers to accept already-resolved `NativeArray ` and pass `kernelProfiles` directly from `TryPrepareValidationJob()`.
Rejected Alternatives: Caching private NativeArray field was rejected because persistent private NativeArray state violates vault law. Leaving duplicate resolution was rejected because hot scheduler should not do repeated global lookups when data is already in scope.
Scalability potential: Low devices remove two redundant main-thread lookups per validation scheduling pass. Middle/High/Ultra behavior is unchanged, while profile scans still scale with fixed small vault capacity.
Hardware Impact: Saves small but real PRE_SIMULATION overhead, estimated below 1-3 us/frame on low-end CPUs depending on vault lookup path. Runtime allocations remain 0 B.
Decision 032 - PRE_SIMULATION Tuning Lookup Collapse
Problem: scheduler resolved quality and tuning through two helper calls that each resolved same tuning vault buffer. This duplicated main-thread service lookup directly before scheduling validation.
Solution: Resolve `NativeArray ` once and pass it to both `ResolveGlobalQualityWeight(NativeArray )` and `ResolveTuning(NativeArray )`. Keep existing no-argument quality helper for other call sites.
Rejected Alternatives: Storing tuning as private persistent field was rejected because all persistent data must stay in vault. Leaving helper duplication was rejected because pre-simulation scheduling already has buffer handle in scope.
Scalability potential: Low devices shave redundant scheduling overhead during command frames. Middle/High/Ultra behavior and quality curve semantics are unchanged.
Hardware Impact: Saves small PRE_SIMULATION overhead, estimated below 1-3 us/frame on weak CPUs. Runtime allocations remain 0 B.
Decision 033 - Tuning Vault Fail-Fast Contract
Problem: After tuning/quality helper cleanup, scheduler could still proceed with default tuning if tuning vault buffer failed to resolve. That hides boot/vault failures and can make command budgets look valid when persistent tuning state is absent.
Solution: Resolve tuning buffer before self-audit and scheduler guard blocks and require `tuningBuffer.IsCreated` before command validation can proceed.
Rejected Alternatives: Silent default tuning was rejected because command budget authority should be explicit vault state, not implicit fallback in active runtime scheduler. Private cached fallback state was rejected by vault law.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra runtime math is unchanged when vault state exists. When vault state is missing, system fails closed rather than running ungoverned command policy.
Hardware Impact: Hot valid path cost is unchanged after previous lookup collapse. Failure path avoids unbounded command processing caused by missing tuning policy.
Decision 034 - Hex-Only Checked-In Kernel Tuning Profiles
Problem: `kernel_tuning_profiles.csv` used opcode names. runtime parser intentionally supports name tokens by hashing ASCII FNV-1a, and current three names hash to intended command-kernel constants. That proof was manual, not enforced. future row such as `TriggerSubtitleCue` would hash to `0x6840BD52`, not route alias constant `0xBCEE082A`, leaving designer tuning inert while CSV appeared valid.
Solution: Change checked-in tuning CSV to exact hex opcode hashes and make `Validate_Mod_API_Static.ps1` require duplicate-free, hex-only profile set containing exactly `SurvivalOverride`, `HapticPulse`, and `SubtitleCue` from `FutureCommandOpcodes`. Keep runtime support for name tokens for external authoring, but repository authority is now hash-stable.
Rejected Alternatives: Keeping name rows was rejected because FNV correctness would remain undocumented convention. Adding runtime remap for arbitrary aliases was rejected because active route already normalizes `TriggerSubtitleCue` to subtitle profile and additional alias policy belongs in static authoring, not hot kernel lookup. Inline comments on data rows were rejected because zero-GC parser does not strip trailing comments from numeric tokens.
Scalability potential: Low devices keep enforced haptic/subtitle caps because exact profile rows must exist. Middle/High/Ultra can raise profile values deliberately, but static validation prevents accidental inert tuning rows.
Hardware Impact: Runtime hot cost is 0 us. Static validation adds cold script parsing only and prevents misconfigured profiles from disabling 50-300 us spam-frame shedding protection.
Decision 035 - Runtime Kernel Tuning Duplicate Rejection
Problem: `TryValidateKernelTuningProfilesCsv()` proved row shape and capacity, but it did not reject duplicate opcode profile rows. Duplicate rows make profile resolution order-dependent because Burst lookup returns first matching `OpcodeHash`, while later rows still occupy vault capacity and mislead designers.
Solution: Add `ContainsKernelTuningProfileBefore()` over existing `ReadOnlySpan ` source and reject any duplicate `OpcodeHash` during validation pass before `MemClearArray(profiles)`.
Rejected Alternatives: Allowing last-row-wins was rejected because hot lookup intentionally exits on first matching profile for bounded scans. Allocating temporary hash set was rejected because CSV reload path already has full scratch span and profile count is bounded.
Scalability potential: Low devices retain deterministic conservative caps under manual CSV edits. Middle/High/Ultra can tune richer haptic/subtitle profiles without hidden row-order semantics.
Hardware Impact: Runtime hot cost is 0 us. Cold reload adds O(rows^2) duplicate scan over tiny profile table; this is acceptable and prevents order-dependent command spam caps.
Decision 036 - Strict Numeric Tuning Parse
Problem: `TryParseKernelTuningCsvLine()` previously used fallback values for malformed numeric tuning tokens. That made CSV transactional only at row/opcode level; bad `MaxPerFrame`, `RangeMeters`, or `IntensityScale` token could still apply profile with defaults and silently change command spam policy.
Solution: Parse all six numeric tuning columns explicitly and return `false` if any token is missing, non-numeric, non-finite, or if trailing non-empty data remains after intensity column. Flags accept either decimal uint or hex uint through strict token parser.
Rejected Alternatives: Keeping defaults for optional authoring was rejected because this file is command policy, not designer cosmetics. Fallbacks hide failures and can weaken low-end command caps. managed CSV library was rejected by zero-GC policy.
Scalability potential: Low devices keep previous known-good caps when designer mistypes numeric policy. Middle/High/Ultra profile increases only apply when whole row is exact.
Hardware Impact: Runtime hot cost is 0 us. Cold reload does stricter token checks in existing scratch scan and prevents silent removal or weakening of 50-300 us spam-frame guard.
Decision 037 - Signed Integer Token Guard
Problem: `TryParseIntAscii()` accepted lone `-` as integer zero because it did not require digit after sign. After strict tuning parsing, that edge case could still let malformed `MaxPerFrame` token apply as zero.
Solution: Require at least one digit after optional negative sign before returning success.
Rejected Alternatives: Special-casing tuning parser only was rejected because shared ASCII int parser should own integer token correctness. Managed parsing was rejected by zero-GC parser requirement.
Scalability potential: Low devices keep previous valid caps when malformed signed token appears. Middle/High/Ultra tuning remains exact and deterministic.
Hardware Impact: Runtime hot cost is 0 us. Cold parser adds one boolean check and prevents bad caps from silently applying.
Decision 038 - Decimal Parser Overflow Rejection
Problem: Decimal uint/int parsers multiplied accumulators without overflow checks. In unchecked C#, very large CSV token could wrap into small valid number and pass strict tuning validation.
Solution: Add pre-multiply overflow guards to `TryParseUIntAscii()` and `TryParseIntAscii()` using `(MaxValue - digit) / 10` bounds.
Rejected Alternatives: Relying on checked arithmetic was rejected because project-wide compiler settings may not enforce it and Burst-oriented code should be explicit. Managed `uint.Parse`/`int.Parse` was rejected by zero-GC parser requirement.
Scalability potential: Low devices keep safe caps on malformed huge tokens. Middle/High/Ultra tuning remains exact and deterministic.
Hardware Impact: Runtime hot cost is 0 us. Cold parser adds one branch per digit and prevents wrapped command policy values.
Decision 039 - Exact Kernel Tuning CSV Column Count
Problem: `TryParseKernelTuningCsvLine()` rejected non-empty trailing data after intensity column, but trailing empty column like `...,1,` could still be accepted because final token ended at line length. Static validation also proved profile hash membership without proving exact row shape.
Solution: Require exactly six CSV delimiters for runtime tuning rows before parsing opcode and numeric policy fields. Extend `Validate_Mod_API_Static.ps1` to require exactly seven columns for each checked-in tuning row and to validate priority, max-per-frame, flags, range, max-duration, and intensity-scale token shapes.
Rejected Alternatives: Leaving trailing empty columns harmless was rejected because command policy must be exact and fail-closed. Adding quote-aware CSV parsing was rejected because current schema is simple numeric policy and quoted fields are not part of contract.
Scalability potential: Low devices keep previous protective caps when malformed authoring row has missing or extra fields. Middle/High/Ultra profile increases apply only from exact seven-column rows.
Hardware Impact: Runtime hot cost is 0 us. Cold parser adds one delimiter scan per tuning row and prevents malformed profile policy from weakening 50-300 us hostile-spam guard.
Decision 040 - Static Tuning Numeric Range Parity
Problem: static validator accepted finite `double` decimal floats and full `int.MinValue`, but runtime parsing stores floats as `float` and signed int parser rejects magnitudes larger than `int.MaxValue`. Static validation could therefore approve rows that runtime parser would fail.
Solution: Tighten `Test-StrictDecimalFloat()` to require absolute value within `[single]::MaxValue`, and tighten `Test-StrictInt32()` to match runtime parser's `[-int.MaxValue, int.MaxValue]` representable range.
Rejected Alternatives: Relying on runtime rejection alone was rejected because static gate is supposed to fail authoring policy before it reaches editor reload facade. Changing runtime to parse `int.MinValue` was rejected because negative max-frame values are not useful policy surface and current parser is intentionally simple.
Scalability potential: Low devices keep previous caps when malformed huge float or signed integer policy appears. Middle/High/Ultra tuning remains exact and static/runtime outcomes match.
Hardware Impact: Runtime hot cost is 0 us. Static validation adds two range comparisons only.
Decision 041 - Semantic Kernel Tuning Range Rejection
Problem: Strict CSV parsing still accepted semantically invalid command policy such as negative priority, zero max-per-frame, negative range, overlong duration, or negative intensity scale. Runtime then silently clamped those values while mutating live `ModKernelTuningProfile` vault. That hides authoring mistakes and can either weaken spam caps or suppress command lanes without hard reload failure.
Solution: Add `IsKernelTuningSemanticRangeValid()` to reject malformed policy before profile DTO creation: `PriorityWeight` must be `[0,1]`, `MaxPerFrame` must be `>= 1`, `RangeMeters` must be `[1,100000]`, `MaxDurationSeconds` must be `[0.01,30]`, and `IntensityScale` must be `>= 0`. DTO now stores validated values directly instead of using clamp/saturate as parser fallback. Static validation enforces same ranges.
Rejected Alternatives: Keeping clamps was rejected because command policy is not cosmetic tolerance; bad CSV must fail closed and preserve previous live vault state. Allowing `MaxPerFrame=0` as "unlimited" was rejected because it silently removes spam cap that protects weak devices. Adding arbitrary intensity upper caps was rejected because downstream math already saturates intensity and no documented authored maximum exists.
Scalability potential: Low devices keep previous conservative haptic/subtitle caps when bad tuning row appears. Middle/High/Ultra can still raise ranges and durations within documented command-kernel envelope, but only through exact validated policy.
Hardware Impact: Runtime hot path remains 0 us. Cold reload adds five range comparisons and prevents malformed CSV from disabling 50-300 us hostile-command shedding protection.
Decision 042 - Babel Localization Static Gate Drift Repair
Problem: `Docs/Modding/Validate_Mod_API_Static.ps1` failed before command-kernel CSV checks because active source had already replaced `HectonAPI.Localization.InjectTable(Dictionary )` with rejected `InjectBabelEnvelope(ReadOnlySpan )`, while Modding schema/audit docs still required `InjectTable`. stale gate would pressure agents to restore runtime dictionary localization injection, contradicting Babel binary authority.
Solution: Align Modding static validator, `Signal_Schema.json`, `Resource_Content_Audit_Matrix.md`, `Mod_API_Specification.md`, and `API_Surface_Audit_Matrix.md` with current rejected `InjectBabelEnvelope` seam. No runtime localization owner code was touched.
Rejected Alternatives: Re-adding `InjectTable` was rejected because runtime dictionary/string localization injection is explicitly disabled and would reintroduce managed localization table mutation. Ignoring static gate failure was rejected because it masked command-kernel CSV validation and left stale API docs as false authority.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra runtime command-kernel behavior is unchanged. static gate now protects envelope-only Mod API route without reopening managed localization injection.
Hardware Impact: Runtime impact is 0 us. Developer-hardware impact is restored static gate usefulness; `Validate_Mod_API_Static.ps1` reaches and proves command-kernel CSV policy again.
Decision 043 - Optional Command Priority Bucket Proof
Problem: `LoadSheddingJob.ResolveDropPriority()` used hard-coded `profileWeight <= 0.30f` threshold for optional shed bucket. checked-in `HapticPulse` profile has priority `0.35`, so haptic spam was classified as standard work and could survive first overflow drop pass ahead of other non-survival standard packets. That violates Task 10's requirement that haptic/subtitle spam be first load shed under thermal pressure.
Solution: Promote shed thresholds into `FutureCommandSandboxConstants.KernelOptionalPriorityMax` and `KernelSurvivalPriorityMin`, with optional max set to `0.50f` and survival min set to `0.90f`. static Mod API gate now parses those constants and proves checked-in `HapticPulse`/`SubtitleCue` priorities stay inside optional bucket while `SurvivalOverride` stays inside protected bucket.
Rejected Alternatives: Editing only CSV haptic priority from `0.35` to `0.30` was rejected because it would keep magic threshold invisible and fragile. Making haptic/subtitle unconditionally optional was rejected because designers still need continuous priority surface for future policy, but checked-in defaults must prove required thermal-shed behavior.
Scalability potential: Low devices now shed both haptic and subtitle traffic before standard packets under polynomial global budget. Middle devices keep cosmetic command throughput bounded. High/Ultra can still tune optional lanes deliberately, but static validation prevents accidental default drift.
Hardware Impact: Runtime hot cost is unchanged: two float comparisons remain two float comparisons. Low-end protection improves by preserving intended 50-300 us hostile-command shedding path for haptic spam.
Decision 044 - Mixed Thermal Shed Telemetry Mask Preservation
Problem: `TryPrepareValidationJob()` records thermal shedding in `statsBuffer[0]`, then clears stats buffer before scheduling `ValidateFutureCommandEnvelopeJob`. On frames where shedding and command processing both happen, `FinalizeValidationTelemetry()` preserved shed count through `validationState.ThermalDropped`, but `ThermalShed` bit was absent from `RejectionMask`. Forensics could therefore show dropped packets without thermal-shed reason flag.
Solution: Merge local `telemetryStats` copy during finalization. If `validationState.ThermalDropped != 0`, OR in `FutureCommandRejectReason.ThermalShed` before writing both generic telemetry and kernel telemetry. Also replace raw `stats.Dropped + validationState.ThermalDropped` with saturating add to avoid uint wrap in pathological long-run spam tests.
Rejected Alternatives: Keeping count-only telemetry was rejected because blackbox ring must support cause reconstruction, not just totals. Storing shedder stats in second persistent buffer was rejected because existing scheduled validation state already carries count and no new Vault buffer is needed.
Scalability potential: Low devices now preserve exact thermal-shed cause flags during mixed shed+process frames. Middle/High/Ultra behavior is unchanged; overkill traffic still reports its shed pressure accurately.
Hardware Impact: One branch and one OR during finalization only. Hot Burst job cost is unchanged. Forensic correctness improves without new allocations or buffers.
Decision 045 - Bounded Kernel Profile MaxPerFrame Authority
Problem: `kernel_tuning_profiles.csv` semantic validation required `MaxPerFrame >= 1` but had no upper bound. malformed or stale Vault profile could carry enormous `MaxPerFrame`, overflow aggregate profile-budget sum, or effectively disable per-opcode spam cap that protects weak devices.
Solution: Add `FutureCommandSandboxConstants.KernelMaxProfileCommandsPerFrame = 10000`. Runtime CSV validation now rejects `max_per_frame` outside `[1,10000]`, static Mod API gate enforces same range, and scheduler defensively clamps existing Vault profile rows before aggregate budget summing, smallest-cap trip checks, and per-opcode cap resolution.
Rejected Alternatives: Trusting CSV parser alone was rejected because profile rows are Vault state and can be stale or externally mutated. Using `int.MaxValue` as authoring ceiling was rejected because it is not frame budget; it is denial of backpressure. Silently clamping during CSV ingestion was rejected because bad command policy must fail closed and preserve previous live profile table.
Scalability potential: Low devices keep hostile-command cap even if profile file or stale Vault row attempts unrealistic budget. Middle/High/Ultra can raise command throughput deliberately up to same bounded scheduler envelope without sacrificing deterministic shedding.
Hardware Impact: Runtime hot cost is few integer min/sub/add operations across at most 16 profile rows during PRE_SIMULATION scheduling, estimated below 1 us on i3/MX350. Prevents overflow-driven loss of 50-300 us hostile-spam protection path.
